bull_bear.body:
- Brand: the "COUNTRY CLUB" brand is described as well accepted and as enjoying the trust of patrons, guests and the neighbourhoods in which it operates its hotels
- Balanced portfolio of owned, leased and managed properties, giving flexibility in how room inventory is added
- Diversified brand architecture across geographies and segments, with a stable stream of fee-based income
- Pan-India footprint across 15 named cities and leisure destinations, giving members multiple location and season choices
- Fire and Life Safety (FLS) audit programme across resorts, hotels and corporate office, with no fatality reported for the year
- Food Safety Management System with external audits against FSSAI guidelines and standards
- Customer-acquisition engine through referrals, alliances and digital leads, plus a product portfolio across all life-stage segments
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Membership receivables and customer credit risk — The Company finances customers' purchase of vacation-ownership and similar products, exposing it to non-payment or delayed payment of membership instalments and annual subscription fees and so to higher outstanding receivables. Management separately expects customer outstandings to rise owing to the liquidity environment. Mitigation cited: higher down payments, shorter EMI tenures, customer profiling and improved collections.
- Funding availability and cost for a capital-intensive resort build-out — Business operations involve significant investments in building resorts, exposing the Company to the timely and adequate availability of funds at competitive rates to finance growth. The Company is concurrently deferring capex and selling down non-operational clubs, resorts and hotels to clear debts and reduce secured loans - i.e. it is funding-constrained today.
- Room-inventory versus member-growth mismatch (service-delivery risk) — Operational risk centres on balancing resort inventory against customer growth over the long service duration of membership products; with multiple location and season choices, a member's first-choice holiday may be unavailable, causing dissatisfaction. Management also flags the ability to consistently attract, retain and motivate managerial talent and skilled personnel in a high-growth industry as an operational risk, with talent availability separately cited as a constraint on industry-wide supply additions. Managed by a judicious mix of greenfield, acquisitions, inventory expansion at existing sites and long-term leases, and by HR practices intended to lift engagement and retention.
- Regulatory, legal and land/property approval risk — Exposure to cumbersome land acquisition, conversion of land for commercial usage, property development, environmental clearances and approvals for new resorts, plus tax proceedings, legal proceedings on properties, customer complaints and non-compliance with hospitality-sector and environmental regulations.
- Foreign exchange and cross-border political/regulatory exposure via overseas subsidiaries — The Company states it is exposed to foreign exchange risk through its overseas subsidiary companies in the Middle East and Sri Lanka, and to political and regulatory risks emanating from its international presence. (Note: the Directors' Report separately reports Foreign Currency Earnings/Inflow and Foreign Currency Expenditure/Outflow as NIL for both 2025-26 and 2024-25, which sits uneasily with a stated FX exposure.)
- Discretionary-demand cyclicality, geopolitical travel disruption and physical/climate exposure at remote resorts — Hospitality and vacation-ownership revenue depends on domestic discretionary spending, inbound travel recovery, air connectivity and corporate/MICE trends. Management flags that West Asia geopolitical developments and related aviation disruptions may hit international and corporate travel corridors near-term while keeping fuel, logistics and utility costs elevated, and that a global financial crisis or deterioration in global trade could adversely affect the Company's performance. Separately, some resorts sit in remote areas where earthquakes, floods and landslides may cut member access, and the Directors' Report flags rising climate-event frequency as increasing operational and infrastructure risk for businesses.
- Cost inflation on resort operations, projects and renovations — Rising inflation could increase the cost of resort operations as well as project and renovation costs. Mitigation cited: centralised procurement of consumables and project inputs, plus price increases passed through as F&B charges and membership fees - the latter itself a demand risk in a discretionary category.
- Governance: absence of a Risk Management Committee and concentrated promoter/family control — The MD&A states the Risk Management Committee is not applicable to the Company, which relies instead on a Risk Management Policy on its website. The Board of 6 has 3 executive directors who are a father and his two sons, the Chairman & Managing Director holds 65.05% of equity, and related-party lease-rent and remuneration transactions run with the promoter family and with wholly owned subsidiaries - so oversight of those dealings rests on 3 independent directors.

outlook.body:
- Grow through a balanced portfolio of owned, leased and managed properties rather than a single ownership model, using greenfield projects, acquisitions, inventory expansion at existing locations and long-term leases as alternatives depending on conditions
- Strengthen the development pipeline by acquiring new resorts and hotels, and pursue opportunistic growth avenues to build a healthy project pipeline across markets
- Prioritise fast-turnaround deals and reduce project launch turnaround times by enhancing agility across processes
- Maximise sell-down of non-operational clubs, resorts and hotels to clear debt and reduce secured loans
- Run a fixed-cost spend-optimisation programme: renegotiate F&B ingredient contracts, rationalise power and fuel by closing open floors/wings, cut corporate overheads and access state-level utility waivers
- Conserve cash by deferring capital expenditure and renovations except essential hotel maintenance
- Drive membership acquisition through referrals, alliances and digital leads, with a product portfolio spanning all life-stage segments and initiatives to augment member spend at resorts
- Improve receivables quality by increasing down payments and lowering EMI tenures on membership financing
- Pass input-cost inflation through to customers via F&B charges and membership fees, supported by centralised procurement of consumables and project inputs
- When evaluating new projects, seek long-term shareholder value through optimal financing and fiscal discipline
- Leverage the COUNTRY CLUB brand and a diversified brand architecture across geographies and segments, with fee-based income as a stable earnings layer
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: ROUTING NOTE: this bundle's MD&A slice is almost entirely India macroeconomic commentary (GDP, CPI, FX reserves, unemployment, sector GVA, Union Budget, RBI policy) and contains no company capex content at all; the only company-specific sentence in this bundle is the Directors'-Report line on room inventory. The cash-conservation, sell-down and acquisition-intent language quoted below is MD&A text that was routed to the profile and risks_esg bundles instead, and is cited here for the expansion picture. The bundle contains no capex or capacity-expansion programme for the Company. The only company-specific expansion statements are qualitative and undated: the Directors' Report states the Company "added significant room inventory in FY 2025-26" without disclosing a room count or a rupee quantum, and the MD&A says the Company is "ideally placed to further strengthen its development potential by acquiring new resorts and hotels in future" while remaining "judicious in the use of different options - greenfield projects, acquisitions, expanding inventory at existing locations, long term leases and inventory arrangements". Against this, the MD&A's own cash-conservation paragraph states the opposite posture for the near term: "deferral of capital expenditure and renovations, unless absolutely required. Capital expenditure is planned to be incurred for essential hotel maintenance", alongside "maximising selling down of non-operational clubs, resorts and hotels across the nation by clearing its debts and reducing the secured loans" - i.e. net asset monetisation rather than a build-out. No named project, no commissioning or ramp timeline, and no rupee amount is disclosed anywhere in this bundle. Note that the capital-expenditure language that dominates this routed bundle ("front-loading of government capital expenditure (CAPEX)", "the government's significantly expanded capital expenditure target for the year", "sustained public capital expenditure") is India's PUBLIC capex in the macroeconomic commentary, not the Company's own, and has been excluded.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Management expects the hospitality sector to remain stable in FY2026-27, supported by domestic leisure travel and MICE demand, with room rates likely to remain firm
- Management cites ICRA projecting industry revenues to grow ~7-9% Y-o-Y in FY2026-27, with occupancy and ARR continuing to improve
- Management cites ICRA projecting hotel demand growth of 8-10% CAGR against supply growth of 5-6% over FY2025-FY2028, with measured supply additions supporting occupancy and ADR
- Medium-to-long-term structural drivers management names: rising discretionary spending, an expanding middle class, and continued business travel
- India's rising global prominence is expected to attract higher foreign visitor inflows, including heads of state and senior business executives
- Company-specific: management says it witnessed an uptick in the Hotel & Hospitality sector, occupancy increased significantly, membership acquisitions recovered from the previous year, and the Company added significant room inventory in FY 2025-26
- Management expects demand to catch up within the year but believes customers will expect relaxed holiday plans
- Management expects some increase in customer outstandings owing to the liquidity environment
- Near-term watch item: geopolitical developments in West Asia and related aviation disruptions could temporarily hit international and corporate travel corridors while keeping fuel, logistics and utility costs elevated
- Policy tailwinds management cites: the GST rate on hotel rooms priced up to Rs 7,500 per day cut to 5% (without input tax credit) effective September 22, 2025, improving affordability in mid-scale and budget segments, albeit with the loss of input tax credit; plus Swadesh Darshan 2.0, PRASHAD and RCS-UDAN connectivity initiatives
- Own-portfolio drivers management names: strong domestic presence, balanced owned/leased/managed property mix, diversified brand architecture, and a stable stream of fee-based income

products.title: Products & brands
products.body:
- **Hospitality:** COUNTRY CLUB (clubs, resorts and hotels), Hospitality at Home (bakery, confectionery and wellness services to homes)
- **Vacation ownership / membership:** Vacation ownership memberships (instalment and annual-subscription based)

end_markets.title: End Markets (RHP)
end_markets.body:
- India — domestic leisure travel
- India — domestic business travel and MICE
- Pan-India presence in Hyderabad, Mumbai, Ahmedabad, Faridabad, Surat, Kolkata, Kochi, Lucknow, Bandipur, Kovalam, Kodaikanal, Jim Corbett, Goa, Chennai and Bengaluru
- Holiday destinations including Goa, Shimla, Jim Corbett and Bandipur
- Middle East (via overseas subsidiary)
- Sri Lanka (via overseas subsidiary)

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Management expects the hospitality sector to remain stable in FY2026-27, supported by domestic leisure travel and MICE demand, with room rates likely to remain firm
- Management cites ICRA projecting industry revenues to grow ~7-9% Y-o-Y in FY2026-27, with occupancy and ARR continuing to improve
- Management cites ICRA projecting hotel demand growth of 8-10% CAGR against supply growth of 5-6% over FY2025-FY2028, with measured supply additions supporting occupancy and ADR
- Medium-to-long-term structural drivers management names: rising discretionary spending, an expanding middle class, and continued business travel
- India's rising global prominence is expected to attract higher foreign visitor inflows, including heads of state and senior business executives
- Company-specific: management says it witnessed an uptick in the Hotel & Hospitality sector, occupancy increased significantly, membership acquisitions recovered from the previous year, and the Company added significant room inventory in FY 2025-26
- Management expects demand to catch up within the year but believes customers will expect relaxed holiday plans
- Management expects some increase in customer outstandings owing to the liquidity environment
- Near-term watch item: geopolitical developments in West Asia and related aviation disruptions could temporarily hit international and corporate travel corridors while keeping fuel, logistics and utility costs elevated
- Policy tailwinds management cites: the GST rate on hotel rooms priced up to Rs 7,500 per day cut to 5% (without input tax credit) effective September 22, 2025, improving affordability in mid-scale and budget segments, albeit with the loss of input tax credit; plus Swadesh Darshan 2.0, PRASHAD and RCS-UDAN connectivity initiatives
- Own-portfolio drivers management names: strong domestic presence, balanced owned/leased/managed property mix, diversified brand architecture, and a stable stream of fee-based income

capital_allocation.title: Strategy & capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
- Grow through a balanced portfolio of owned, leased and managed properties rather than a single ownership model, using greenfield projects, acquisitions, inventory expansion at existing locations and long-term leases as alternatives depending on conditions
- Strengthen the development pipeline by acquiring new resorts and hotels, and pursue opportunistic growth avenues to build a healthy project pipeline across markets
- Prioritise fast-turnaround deals and reduce project launch turnaround times by enhancing agility across processes
- Maximise sell-down of non-operational clubs, resorts and hotels to clear debt and reduce secured loans
- Run a fixed-cost spend-optimisation programme: renegotiate F&B ingredient contracts, rationalise power and fuel by closing open floors/wings, cut corporate overheads and access state-level utility waivers
- Conserve cash by deferring capital expenditure and renovations except essential hotel maintenance
- Drive membership acquisition through referrals, alliances and digital leads, with a product portfolio spanning all life-stage segments and initiatives to augment member spend at resorts
- Improve receivables quality by increasing down payments and lowering EMI tenures on membership financing
- Pass input-cost inflation through to customers via F&B charges and membership fees, supported by centralised procurement of consumables and project inputs
- When evaluating new projects, seek long-term shareholder value through optimal financing and fiscal discipline
- Leverage the COUNTRY CLUB brand and a diversified brand architecture across geographies and segments, with fee-based income as a stable earnings layer

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: ROUTING NOTE: this bundle's MD&A slice is almost entirely India macroeconomic commentary (GDP, CPI, FX reserves, unemployment, sector GVA, Union Budget, RBI policy) and contains no company capex content at all; the only company-specific sentence in this bundle is the Directors'-Report line on room inventory. The cash-conservation, sell-down and acquisition-intent language quoted below is MD&A text that was routed to the profile and risks_esg bundles instead, and is cited here for the expansion picture. The bundle contains no capex or capacity-expansion programme for the Company. The only company-specific expansion statements are qualitative and undated: the Directors' Report states the Company "added significant room inventory in FY 2025-26" without disclosing a room count or a rupee quantum, and the MD&A says the Company is "ideally placed to further strengthen its development potential by acquiring new resorts and hotels in future" while remaining "judicious in the use of different options - greenfield projects, acquisitions, expanding inventory at existing locations, long term leases and inventory arrangements". Against this, the MD&A's own cash-conservation paragraph states the opposite posture for the near term: "deferral of capital expenditure and renovations, unless absolutely required. Capital expenditure is planned to be incurred for essential hotel maintenance", alongside "maximising selling down of non-operational clubs, resorts and hotels across the nation by clearing its debts and reducing the secured loans" - i.e. net asset monetisation rather than a build-out. No named project, no commissioning or ramp timeline, and no rupee amount is disclosed anywhere in this bundle. Note that the capital-expenditure language that dominates this routed bundle ("front-loading of government capital expenditure (CAPEX)", "the government's significantly expanded capital expenditure target for the year", "sustained public capital expenditure") is India's PUBLIC capex in the macroeconomic commentary, not the Company's own, and has been excluded.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Brand: the "COUNTRY CLUB" brand is described as well accepted and as enjoying the trust of patrons, guests and the neighbourhoods in which it operates its hotels
- Balanced portfolio of owned, leased and managed properties, giving flexibility in how room inventory is added
- Diversified brand architecture across geographies and segments, with a stable stream of fee-based income
- Pan-India footprint across 15 named cities and leisure destinations, giving members multiple location and season choices
- Fire and Life Safety (FLS) audit programme across resorts, hotels and corporate office, with no fatality reported for the year
- Food Safety Management System with external audits against FSSAI guidelines and standards
- Customer-acquisition engine through referrals, alliances and digital leads, plus a product portfolio across all life-stage segments

risks.title: Bear — key risks
risks.body:
- Membership receivables and customer credit risk — The Company finances customers' purchase of vacation-ownership and similar products, exposing it to non-payment or delayed payment of membership instalments and annual subscription fees and so to higher outstanding receivables. Management separately expects customer outstandings to rise owing to the liquidity environment. Mitigation cited: higher down payments, shorter EMI tenures, customer profiling and improved collections.
- Funding availability and cost for a capital-intensive resort build-out — Business operations involve significant investments in building resorts, exposing the Company to the timely and adequate availability of funds at competitive rates to finance growth. The Company is concurrently deferring capex and selling down non-operational clubs, resorts and hotels to clear debts and reduce secured loans - i.e. it is funding-constrained today.
- Room-inventory versus member-growth mismatch (service-delivery risk) — Operational risk centres on balancing resort inventory against customer growth over the long service duration of membership products; with multiple location and season choices, a member's first-choice holiday may be unavailable, causing dissatisfaction. Management also flags the ability to consistently attract, retain and motivate managerial talent and skilled personnel in a high-growth industry as an operational risk, with talent availability separately cited as a constraint on industry-wide supply additions. Managed by a judicious mix of greenfield, acquisitions, inventory expansion at existing sites and long-term leases, and by HR practices intended to lift engagement and retention.
- Regulatory, legal and land/property approval risk — Exposure to cumbersome land acquisition, conversion of land for commercial usage, property development, environmental clearances and approvals for new resorts, plus tax proceedings, legal proceedings on properties, customer complaints and non-compliance with hospitality-sector and environmental regulations.
- Foreign exchange and cross-border political/regulatory exposure via overseas subsidiaries — The Company states it is exposed to foreign exchange risk through its overseas subsidiary companies in the Middle East and Sri Lanka, and to political and regulatory risks emanating from its international presence. (Note: the Directors' Report separately reports Foreign Currency Earnings/Inflow and Foreign Currency Expenditure/Outflow as NIL for both 2025-26 and 2024-25, which sits uneasily with a stated FX exposure.)
- Discretionary-demand cyclicality, geopolitical travel disruption and physical/climate exposure at remote resorts — Hospitality and vacation-ownership revenue depends on domestic discretionary spending, inbound travel recovery, air connectivity and corporate/MICE trends. Management flags that West Asia geopolitical developments and related aviation disruptions may hit international and corporate travel corridors near-term while keeping fuel, logistics and utility costs elevated, and that a global financial crisis or deterioration in global trade could adversely affect the Company's performance. Separately, some resorts sit in remote areas where earthquakes, floods and landslides may cut member access, and the Directors' Report flags rising climate-event frequency as increasing operational and infrastructure risk for businesses.
- Cost inflation on resort operations, projects and renovations — Rising inflation could increase the cost of resort operations as well as project and renovation costs. Mitigation cited: centralised procurement of consumables and project inputs, plus price increases passed through as F&B charges and membership fees - the latter itself a demand risk in a discretionary category.
- Governance: absence of a Risk Management Committee and concentrated promoter/family control — The MD&A states the Risk Management Committee is not applicable to the Company, which relies instead on a Risk Management Policy on its website. The Board of 6 has 3 executive directors who are a father and his two sons, the Chairman & Managing Director holds 65.05% of equity, and related-party lease-rent and remuneration transactions run with the promoter family and with wholly owned subsidiaries - so oversight of those dealings rests on 3 independent directors.
